title: Interactive and Experiential Art
answer: Audience-reactive installations, generative AR and VR, dialogue engines, data sculptures and audio-visual systems.

children.name: Audience-Reactive Installations
children.blurb: Audience-reactive installations are artworks that sense the people in the room and change what they show, play or do in response.

children.name: Generative AR and VR Environments
children.blurb: Generative AR and VR environments cover systems that build or alter three dimensional scenes, avatars and spatial effects in real time, whether the viewer sees them through a headset, a phone camera or a projection.

children.name: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
children.blurb: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are conversational systems built to guide visitors through exhibitions, museums, galleries and public art installations.

children.name: Data Sculpture
children.blurb: Data Sculpture is the practice of turning a dataset into a physical or spatial object that a viewer can walk around, touch, or hear.

children.name: Audio-Visual Systems
children.blurb: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image are generated, processed or synchronised together, often in response to the presence or actions of an audience.

sections.body: Interactive and experiential art covers work where the audience is part of the system rather than a viewer standing outside it. In practice, artists use cameras, microphones, depth sensors and motion tracking to feed live signals into models that respond in real time, so the piece changes with each person who enters the room. Generative systems produce imagery, sound or text on the fly, and the artist's role shifts toward designing rules, training data and the boundaries of what the system can do. Dialogue engines let visitors talk with a character or a guide, and audio-visual systems tie sound and image together so that one drives the other. The field is less about finished objects and more about behaviour that unfolds over the duration of an encounter.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The technical side is largely workable. Real-time tracking, projection mapping, spatial audio and generative models are all available to artists without a research lab, and the site tracks 1000 live image generation models and 2000 audio models that such work can draw on. What is not solved is meaning. A system that reacts is easy, a system that reacts in a way that feels authored and worth returning to is hard, and much of the field's output is technically impressive for a few minutes and thin after that. Latency, calibration and the cost of running models on site remain practical obstacles, and installations often need a technician present for the run of a show. Rights and consent are unsettled too, with 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, 18 of them involving AI music services, and audience data captured by sensors raises questions most exhibitors have not answered. Nothing here is settled enough to call a standard practice.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages divide by the kind of signal the work is built on. Audience-Reactive Installations is the entry point for pieces driven by presence and movement, and it is where a reader should start to understand the basic loop of sensing, interpretation and response. Generative AR and VR Environments takes that loop into headset and phone based space, where the audience moves through a constructed world rather than standing in front of one. Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents covers the conversational strand, including characters and guides that speak with visitors, and it is the page to read for questions about language models in a gallery or museum setting. Data Sculpture handles work that turns datasets into physical or spatial form, which is where the ethical and interpretive arguments tend to concentrate. Audio-Visual Systems is the cross-cutting page for sound and image working together, and it is useful for readers interested in the technical and compositional side rather than the narrative one.
